description: Hello! We’re Mario, Víctor, Eduardo and Belén, a multidisciplinary team from different parts of Spain. None of us are aerospacial experts, but we’re really excited to take on the NASA Flame in Freefall challenge! Fire behaves very differently without gravity, and that matters as we plan to live on the Moon and Mars. This weekend we’ll dive into NASA’s combustion data and try to turn it into something useful for keeping astronauts, and people on Earth, safe. Good luck to everyone!
summary:
IGNIS-SI is a web application that turns NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion experiments into something a mission planner can explore in minutes instead of weeks. 
Since the data is hard to find, hard to compare and hard to interpret, IGNIS-SI offers three connected tools: 
1. An interactive, animated simulator where users change experiment variables (gravity level, atmosphere, oxygen concentration or pressure, among others) and see how flame behavior changes across environments.

2. Natural-language search: an LLM served with Ollama queries a structured SQLite database of PSI investigations, so a question like “how does low oxygen affect flame spread?” returns the most relevant experiments with their DOIs. It runs in the cloud today; a future version will run fully offline, as crews far from Earth will need.

3. A research tab linking current microgravity combustion studies to future research  of next-generation fire safety controls and equipment for cabins, and bases on the lunar and Martian surfaces. Futhermore, on Earth, possible applications are included to support fire-safety decisions.
details:
IGNIS-SI


IGNIS-SI is a web application that turns NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data into answers for mission designers, researchers and fire-safety engineers. It is built on 24 PSI investigations, normalized and validated by the team, and organized in three connected tabs.

0. How we built the dataset. Before building the web application, we built an AI pipeline to classify and tag NASA’s data. PSI data comes in two forms, so it was processed in two ways:

  • Text and numerical data. A Python script filters the PSI catalog by Combustion Science, keeping the 24 target investigations and their official DOIs. The raw records are then cleaned and classified with a VLM (qwen2.5:vl via Ollama).
  • Experiment videos. PSI videos contain information that no table records, so we trained a custom YOLO model to annotate them automatically.

With the dataset in place, we built the web application on top of it.

1. Simulator, an interactive digital twin. The user sets oxygen concentration (21–85 %), cabin pressure (4.3–14.7 psi), forced airflow and gravity level (0g orbit, 0.16g Moon, 0.38g Mars, 1g Earth). They can also load preset atmospheres sourced from NASA documents, such as the ISS cabin or the recommended exploration atmosphere of 34 % O₂ at 8.2 psi. A 3D scene responds immediately: a flame, a spacecraft cabin, or a lunar or Martian habitat. The flame shape, colour and soot follow the regimes described in PSI experiments, such as spherical diffusion flames in still 0g air or inverse flames at high oxygen.

The evidence underneath is real data. Every investigation is ranked by how closely its tested conditions match the user’s environment, using the following weighted score: oxygen 35 %, pressure 25 %, gravity 25 %, airflow 15 % (the reasoning behind these weights is explained at the end). Each result is labelled Covers, Bounds, Partial or Outside. One example: no fire has yet been tested at lunar or Martian gravity, so those cases are bounded by 0g and 1g data.

2. Library, a natural-language search. PSI records and raw data files were organized into a SQLite database, using the tags assigned by our AI pipeline. When a user asks a question in everyday language, a language model (qwen2.5 via Ollama) interprets it and runs two searches in parallel: a semantic search, and a tag-based search that maps the question onto the same tag taxonomy used to classify the data. Exact matching on titles, PSI IDs and mission acronyms such as FLEX, BASS or Saffire runs alongside them, so search still works when the LLM is offline. Matching investigations are ranked, and the raw data files behind them light up in an interactive 3D knowledge graph. Every result links back to its original PSI record and DOI, so it can be checked.

3. Applications, from orbit to Earth. This tab shows what microgravity fire research gives in two directions:

  • Next-generation fire-safety equipment for crewed habitats: smoke detectors sized for orbital smoke, clean-agent suppression, and material screening for exploration atmospheres.
  • Fire safety on Earth: dust-tolerant fire detectors, fine-water-mist extinguishers, lighter firefighter air tanks, and fire-resistant protective clothing.

The main benefit is that decades of experiments can be compared and visualized in one place. Without it, someone would have to read each record and extract the relevant conditions by hand. IGNIS-SI also shows where the evidence stops. When a user sets up a lunar habitat, the app makes it clear that no fire has ever been tested at lunar gravity, and that no investigation in the catalog went below 10.2 psi. The interface needs no specialist knowledge, so engineers, students and the public can all use it. The intended impact is to help mission designers see quickly which experiments support a given spacecraft or habitat atmosphere and where new testing is needed, as missions to the Moon and Mars move to oxygen-enriched, low-pressure cabins.

What makes IGNIS-SI original is the path from raw tables and documents to an interactive experience. Users can watch a flame change as the environment changes, explore the data as a 3D knowledge graph, and ask questions in plain language. Because the LLM runs locally through Ollama, the tool stays free and does not depend on paid external APIs.



Behind the weights
Oxygen carries the most weight (35%) because it is the strongest driver of material flammability and the main new hazard of exploration atmospheres. Gravity (25%) matters because, without it, hot air does not rise and flames behave differently enough that 1g tests cannot stand in for 0g. Pressure (25%) is weighted below oxygen because flammability tracks oxygen fraction more closely than total pressure. Airflow (15%) is physically important in microgravity, where it is what brings fresh oxygen to the flame, but cabin ventilation spans a narrow range and many investigations do not report it, so it carries less weight in the match. These are expert-judgement weights, shown openly, not calibrated coefficients.
